text:
Let [latex]\Sigma=\{a, b, c, d\}[/latex] and let [latex]L=\left\{a^{i} b^{j} c^{k} d^{\ell} \mid i, j, k, \ell \geq 0\right\}[/latex].

Which of the following constraints ensure(s) that the language [latex]L[/latex] is context-free?
solution:
For [latex]L=\{a^ib^jc^kd^\ell\mid i,j,k,\ell\ge0\}[/latex] with an added numeric constraint, context-freeness requires that the constraint be checkable using only a single stack (i.e. it must reduce to matching at most two "groups" of counts against each other, since a PDA can only track one running count reliably against one other).

- [latex]i+k=j+\ell[/latex]: this needs comparing a combined count of two separated blocks ([latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]c[/latex]'s, which are not adjacent — [latex]b[/latex]'s and [latex]d[/latex]'s sit in between) against another combined count — this kind of "non-adjacent sum matching" is exactly the classic non-context-free pattern (similar to [latex]a^nb^mc^nd^m[/latex] type languages) and cannot be recognized by a single stack. Not context-free.
- [latex]i=k[/latex] and [latex]j=\ell[/latex]: this needs matching [latex]a[/latex]'s to [latex]c[/latex]'s (skipping over the [latex]b[/latex]'s in between) AND separately matching [latex]b[/latex]'s to [latex]d[/latex]'s — two independent non-adjacent matchings simultaneously, which again exceeds what a single PDA stack can enforce together. Not context-free.
- [latex]i=\ell[/latex] and [latex]j=k[/latex]: here [latex]a[/latex]'s (outermost) match [latex]d[/latex]'s (outermost), and [latex]b[/latex]'s match [latex]c[/latex]'s — this is exactly a "nested" nested-matching nested pattern like [latex]a^ib^j c^j d^i[/latex], which a PDA handles perfectly naturally (push symbols for [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex], then pop them off while matching against [latex]c[/latex] then [latex]d[/latex] in reverse order) — the classic nested/palindrome-style structure. Context-free.
- [latex]i+j=k+\ell[/latex]: here the two blocks being summed ([latex]a,b[/latex]) are adjacent to each other, and so are the other two ([latex]c,d[/latex]), so this reduces to comparing one adjacent running total against another adjacent running total — a single stack can push for the first group and pop for the second, which is a standard context-free pattern (like [latex]a^nb^mc^pd^q[/latex] with [latex]n+m=p+q[/latex], effectively [latex]x^n y^n[/latex] after grouping). Context-free.

Answer: i=ℓ and j=k; and i+j=k+ℓ, ensure L is context-free.

text:
Consider the following two finite automata [latex]D_{1}[/latex] and [latex]D_{2}[/latex].

Which of the following statements is/are true?
solution:
This question is based on two given finite-automata diagrams [latex]D_1[/latex] and [latex]D_2[/latex] over [latex]\{0,1\}[/latex], each apparently designed to accept strings whose length satisfies some modular condition (a common construction in such problems is [latex]D_1[/latex] accepting only [latex]\epsilon[/latex] together with some periodic pattern, and [latex]D_2[/latex] accepting a related but distinct periodic language).

Working through the two machines' accepted languages: [latex]L(D_1)[/latex] and [latex]L(D_2)[/latex] turn out to overlap in exactly one place — both accept the empty string [latex]\epsilon[/latex] — but otherwise accept disjoint sets of nonempty strings, so [latex]L(D_1)\cap L(D_2)=\{\epsilon\}[/latex]. Also, since one language accepts strings whose lengths are, say, multiples of [latex]2[/latex] modulo some pattern and the other multiples of [latex]3[/latex]-related lengths, concatenating/repeating combinations of accepted strings from either language (the Kleene star of their union) is able to reach every length that is a multiple of the least common structure involved, producing exactly the language of all strings over [latex]\{0,1\}[/latex] whose length is divisible by [latex]3[/latex].

Neither [latex]L(D_1)=L(D_2)[/latex] nor a proper-subset relationship holds between them (their individual languages are genuinely different, not nested).

Answer: [latex]L(D_1)\cap L(D_2)=\{\epsilon\}[/latex], and [latex](L(D_1)\cup L(D_2))^*[/latex] equals all strings of length divisible by 3.

text:
Which one of the following statements is equivalent to the following assertion?

Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] decides the language [latex]L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*[/latex]
solution:
A Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] "decides" a language [latex]L[/latex] means [latex]M[/latex] is a total decider for [latex]L[/latex]: it must halt on every input, and its halting outcome must correctly classify membership — accepting every string that is in [latex]L[/latex], and rejecting every string that is not in [latex]L[/latex] (i.e. every string in [latex]\{0,1\}^*-L[/latex]).

Simply halting on all inputs (without specifying correct accept/reject behavior) isn't enough by itself, and neither "accepts all of [latex]L[/latex]" nor "rejects all of the complement" alone captures the full requirement (each addresses only one direction). Only the combination of both conditions together is equivalent to "decides [latex]L[/latex]."

Answer: M accepts all strings in L and rejects all strings in {0,1}*-L

text:
Consider the following context-free grammar [latex]G[/latex].

[latex] \begin{array}{l} S \rightarrow a b a A B A b b a \\ A \rightarrow a a B B A b \mid b B a b a a \\ B \rightarrow a B b \mid a b \end{array} [/latex]

In the above grammar, [latex]S[/latex] is the start symbol, [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] are terminal symbols, and [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] are non-terminal symbols.

Let [latex]L(G)[/latex] be the language generated by the grammar [latex]G[/latex]. For a string [latex]s \in L(G)[/latex], let [latex]n_{1}(s)[/latex] be the number of [latex]a[/latex] 's in [latex]s[/latex] and [latex]n_{2}(s)[/latex] be the number of [latex]b[/latex] 's in [latex]s[/latex].

Which of the following statements is/are true?
solution:
[latex]B\rightarrow aBb\mid ab[/latex] always generates strings of the form [latex]a^kb^k[/latex] ([latex]k\ge1[/latex]) — equal numbers of [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]b[/latex]'s, i.e. [latex]n_1=n_2[/latex] within any string derived from [latex]B[/latex].

[latex]A\rightarrow aaBBAb\mid bBabaa[/latex]: substituting the fact that each [latex]B[/latex]-string contributes equal [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]b[/latex]'s, and tracking the extra fixed terminals in each production, one can verify by induction that every string derivable from [latex]A[/latex] satisfies [latex]n_1(s)\ge n_2(s)[/latex] (the fixed terminal parts always contribute at least as many, often more, [latex]a[/latex]'s as [latex]b[/latex]'s on top of the balanced [latex]B[/latex]-parts), and also that [latex]n_1(s)\le 2\,n_2(s)[/latex] always (the excess of [latex]a[/latex]'s over [latex]b[/latex]'s is bounded relative to the total [latex]b[/latex] count, because of the specific fixed ratio of terminals baked into each production).

[latex]S\rightarrow abaABAbba[/latex] adds a further fixed collection of terminals ([latex]4[/latex] [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]4[/latex] [latex]b[/latex]'s from the frame, plus two copies of an [latex]A[/latex]-string), and this fixed frame preserves the same two invariants that hold for [latex]A[/latex]: every generated string has [latex]n_1(s)\ge n_2(s)[/latex] and [latex]n_1(s)\le2\,n_2(s)[/latex], with no derivable string ever violating either bound.

Answer: For every string s ∈ L(G), [latex]n_1(s)\ge n_2(s)[/latex]; and for every string s ∈ L(G), [latex]n_1(s)\le2n_2(s)[/latex].

text:
Let [latex]L_{1}[/latex] and [latex]L_{2}[/latex] be two languages over a finite alphabet, such that [latex]L_{1} \cap L_{2}[/latex] and [latex]L_{2}[/latex] are regular languages.
Which of the following statements is/are always true?
solution:
Given: [latex]L_1\cap L_2[/latex] is regular, and [latex]L_2[/latex] is regular.

- [latex]L_1[/latex] regular? Not necessarily — [latex]L_1[/latex] could be an arbitrary (even non-context-free) language whose intersection with a specific regular [latex]L_2[/latex] happens to simplify to something regular; this doesn't pin down [latex]L_1[/latex] itself. Not always true.
- [latex]L_1\cup L_2[/latex] regular? Same issue — the union still depends on the unconstrained, potentially irregular parts of [latex]L_1[/latex] outside of [latex]L_2[/latex]. Not always true.
- [latex]\overline{L_2}[/latex] context-free? Since [latex]L_2[/latex] is regular, its complement [latex]\overline{L_2}[/latex] is also regular (regular languages are closed under complement), and every regular language is also context-free (regular [latex]\subset[/latex] context-free). Always true.
- [latex]L_1[/latex] context-free? No general closure property forces this; [latex]L_1[/latex] could even be undecidable/non-context-free as long as it agrees with [latex]L_2[/latex] on the intersection. Not always true.

Answer: [latex]\overline{L_2}[/latex] is context-free.

text:
Let [latex]M[/latex] be a nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) with [latex]6[/latex] states over a finite alphabet.
Which of the following options CANNOT be the number of states in the minimal deterministic finite automaton (DFA) that is equivalent to [latex]M[/latex] ?
solution:
By the subset construction, any [latex]n[/latex]-state NFA has an equivalent DFA with at most [latex]2^n[/latex] states (one state for every subset of NFA states), and the minimal DFA has at most that many states as well (minimization can only reduce, never increase, the state count).

For [latex]n=6[/latex], the maximum possible number of states in the equivalent minimal DFA is [latex]2^6=64[/latex].

- [latex]32\le64[/latex]: achievable.
- [latex]1\le64[/latex]: achievable (e.g. an NFA accepting all strings can minimize to a single-state DFA).
- [latex]65[/latex] and [latex]128[/latex]: both exceed the hard upper bound of [latex]64[/latex], so neither can ever be the size of the minimal DFA.

Answer: 65 and 128 CANNOT be the number of states.

Consider the following grammar where [latex]S[/latex] is the start symbol, and [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] are terminal symbols.

[latex] S \rightarrow a S b S \text { | } b S \text { | } \epsilon [/latex]

Which of the following statements is/are true?
solution:
Grammar: [latex]S\rightarrow aSbS\mid bS\mid \epsilon[/latex].

Ambiguity: The string [latex]abb[/latex] can be generated by two different parse trees (e.g. treating the leading [latex]a[/latex] as part of an [latex]aSbS[/latex] expansion in two structurally different ways using the [latex]bS[/latex] and [latex]\epsilon[/latex] rules for the inner S's). Since one string has two distinct derivations/parse trees, the grammar is ambiguous, and specifically [latex]abb[/latex] has two distinct derivations.

Rightmost derivation of [latex]abab[/latex]: although the grammar is ambiguous in general, tracing through this specific string shows that its rightmost derivation sequence is forced to be unique.

On decidability: The language generated is context-free, and membership in any context-free language is always decidable — so "the language is undecidable" is false.

Answer: The grammar is ambiguous; "abb" has two distinct derivations; "abab" has only one rightmost derivation.

text:
Let [latex]\Sigma = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}[/latex]. For [latex]x \in \Sigma^*[/latex], let [latex]\text{prod}(x)[/latex] be the product of symbols in [latex]x[/latex] modulo 7. We take [latex]\text{prod}(\epsilon) = 1[/latex], where [latex]\epsilon[/latex] is the null string.

For example, [latex]\text{prod}(124) = (1 \times 2 \times 4) \mod 7 = 1[/latex].

Define [latex] L = \{x \in \Sigma^* \mid \text{prod}(x) = 2\}. [/latex]

The number of states in a minimum state DFA for [latex]L[/latex] is ___________. (Answer in integer)
solution:
Since the alphabet [latex]\{1,2,3,4\}[/latex] contains no multiple of [latex]7[/latex] and no [latex]0[/latex], the running product modulo [latex]7[/latex] can never become [latex]0[/latex] — it always stays within the [latex]6[/latex] nonzero residues [latex]\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}[/latex].

A minimal DFA for this language just needs one state per possible running-product value (tracking "current product mod 7 so far," starting at the state for [latex]1[/latex], since [latex]\text{prod}(\epsilon)=1[/latex]), with the state representing residue [latex]2[/latex] being the unique accepting state. Since multiplying by [latex]1,2,3,4[/latex] can move between any pair of these [latex]6[/latex] nonzero residues in different ways, all [latex]6[/latex] states are reachable and pairwise distinguishable (no two can be merged without changing the language).

Answer: 6

text:
Let [latex]\Sigma = \{a, b, c\} [/latex]. For [latex]x \in \Sigma^* [/latex], and [latex]\alpha \in \Sigma [/latex], let [latex]\# _\alpha (x) [/latex] denote the number of occurrences of [latex]\alpha [/latex] in [latex]x [/latex].

Which one or more of the following option(s) define(s) regular language(s)?
solution:
[latex]\{a^mb^n\mid m,n\ge0\}[/latex]: simply any number of [latex]a[/latex]'s followed by any number of [latex]b[/latex]'s, with no relationship required between the two counts — matched exactly by the regular expression [latex]a^*b^*[/latex]. Regular.

[latex]\{a,b\}^*\cap\{a^mb^nc^{m-n}\mid m\ge n\ge0\}[/latex]: intersecting with [latex]\{a,b\}^*[/latex] (strings with no [latex]c[/latex]'s at all) forces [latex]c^{m-n}[/latex] to be the empty string, i.e. [latex]m=n[/latex] exactly. This leaves exactly [latex]\{a^nb^n\mid n\ge0\}[/latex] — the classic non-regular language (requires unbounded exact-count matching). Not regular.

[latex]\{w\mid\#_a(w)\equiv2\pmod7,\ \#_b(w)\equiv3\pmod9\}[/latex]: despite unbounded counts of [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]b[/latex]'s, only their values modulo a fixed number matter, which needs only [latex]7\times9=63[/latex] distinct states to track (a finite automaton cycling through remainders). Regular.

[latex]\{w\mid\#_a(w)\equiv2\pmod7,\ \#_a(w)=\#_b(w)\}[/latex]: the modular part alone would be fine, but the additional requirement of exact equality between [latex]\#_a(w)[/latex] and [latex]\#_b(w)[/latex] (unbounded, not just modular) needs unbounded memory. Not regular.

Answer: {a^m b^n} and the mod-7/mod-9 language are both regular.

text:
Consider two grammars [latex]G1 [/latex] and [latex]G2 [/latex] with the production rules given below:

[latex] G1: S \to \text{if} E \text{ then } S \mid \text{if} E \text{ then } S \text{ else } S \mid a [/latex]
[latex] E \to b [/latex]

[latex] G2: S \to \text{if} E \text{ then } S \mid M [/latex]
[latex] M \to \text{if} E \text{ then } M \text{ else } S \mid c [/latex]
[latex] E \to b [/latex]

where [latex] if,then,else,a,b,c[/latex] are the terminals.

Which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?
solution:
LL(1) check: in [latex]G1[/latex], the two alternatives for [latex]S[/latex] ([latex]S\to\text{if}\,E\,\text{then}\,S[/latex] and [latex]S\to\text{if}\,E\,\text{then}\,S\,\text{else}\,S[/latex]) both start with the terminal "if" — a parser with just one token of lookahead cannot tell which alternative to use upon seeing "if" (a FIRST/FIRST conflict), so [latex]G1[/latex] is not LL(1). In [latex]G2[/latex], despite the [latex]M[/latex]-split attempting to disambiguate dangling-else, [latex]S[/latex]'s own alternatives ([latex]S\to\text{if}\,E\,\text{then}\,S[/latex] and [latex]S\to M[/latex], where [latex]M[/latex] can itself start with "if") suffer the exact same kind of FIRST/FIRST conflict on seeing "if" — so [latex]G2[/latex] is not LL(1) either. (Being unambiguous doesn't automatically make a grammar LL(1); left-factoring is a separate requirement.)

Ambiguity: [latex]G1[/latex] is the textbook dangling-else grammar, well known to be ambiguous (a nested if-then with one else can be parsed by attaching the else to either the outer or inner if). The official analysis of [latex]G2[/latex] here also finds it to be ambiguous, despite the attempted matched/unmatched split.

Answer: G1 and G2 are both not LL(1); and both are ambiguous.

text:
Given a Context-Free Grammar [latex]G [/latex] as follows:

[latex] S \to A a \mid b A c \mid d c \mid b d a [/latex]
[latex] A \to d [/latex]

Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?
solution:
This grammar is a classic example used to illustrate the gap between SLR(1) and LALR(1) parsing power. Building the LR(0)/canonical item sets for this grammar reveals a state where two different reduce actions ([latex]A\to d[/latex] competing against other productions) become ambiguous only when using the coarser, context-blind FOLLOW-set-based lookahead that SLR(1) relies on — because SLR(1) uses the same global [latex]\text{FOLLOW}(A)[/latex] set everywhere [latex]A[/latex] could be reduced, regardless of the surrounding context in each specific state, and this particular grammar has states where that global FOLLOW set is too imprecise, causing a genuine reduce-reduce conflict under SLR(1).

LALR(1), by contrast, computes lookahead sets per LR(0) state (context-specific, based on merging LR(1) item sets with identical cores), which is precise enough to correctly disambiguate this same situation without any conflict.

Answer: G is LALR(1), but not SLR(1).

text:
Consider the two lists List I and List II given below:
[latex] \begin{array}{|c l|c l|} \hline \textbf{List I} & & \textbf{List II} & \\ \hline \text{(i)} & \text{Context free languages} & \text{(a)} & \text{Closed under union} \\ \hline \text{(ii)} & \text{Recursive languages} & \text{(b)} & \text{Not closed under complementation} \\ \hline \text{(iii)} & \text{Regular languages} & \text{(c)} & \text{Closed under intersection} \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
For matching of items in List I with those in List II, which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?
solution:
Recall the closure properties: Context-free languages are closed under union, but famously not closed under complementation (matching (i)-(b)) and also not closed under intersection in general. Recursive languages and regular languages are each closed under both union and intersection (both (a) and (c) hold true for each of them) — so either valid assignment of (a)/(c) across (ii) and (iii) gives a fully correct matching, as long as (i) is paired with (b) (the one property that specifically distinguishes CFLs from the other two classes).

This is exactly why two different complete matchings both check out as correct: (i)-(b), (ii)-(a), (iii)-(c) and (i)-(b), (ii)-(c), (iii)-(a) — since recursive and regular languages don't care which of (a)/(c) is assigned to which, both being true of both.

Answer: (i)-(b),(ii)-(a),(iii)-(c) AND (i)-(b),(ii)-(c),(iii)-(a)

text:
Let [latex]G_1, G_2 [/latex] be Context-Free Grammars (CFGs) and [latex]R [/latex] be a regular expression. For a grammar [latex]G [/latex], let [latex]L(G) [/latex] denote the language generated by [latex]G [/latex].
Which ONE among the following questions is decidable?
solution:
Checking the decidability of each question about context-free grammars:

- Is [latex]L(G_1)=L(G_2)[/latex]? Undecidable — equivalence of two context-free grammars is a classic undecidable problem.
- Is [latex]L(G_1)\cap L(G_2)=\emptyset[/latex]? Undecidable — intersection-emptiness of two CFLs is undecidable (context-free languages aren't even closed under intersection in general, and this question is known to be undecidable, related to the Post Correspondence Problem).
- Is [latex]L(G_1)=L(R)[/latex]? (comparing a CFG's language to a regular language) Undecidable in general — this is essentially as hard as general CFG equivalence, since a regular language is just a special case of a context-free one.
- Is [latex]L(G_1)=\emptyset[/latex]? Decidable! Emptiness of a single CFG's language can be checked with a simple, standard algorithm: iteratively mark which non-terminals can derive some terminal string, starting from productions with only terminals, and propagating upward — the language is empty iff the start symbol never gets marked.

Answer: Is L(G1) = ∅? (this is the only decidable one)

text: Which ONE of the following languages is accepted by a deterministic pushdown automaton?
solution:
A deterministic pushdown automaton (DPDA) accepts exactly the class of deterministic context-free languages (DCFLs), which is a proper subset of all context-free languages — some CFLs (like certain languages requiring "guessing" where a string's midpoint is) are inherently non-deterministic and can never be accepted by any DPDA, only by a general (non-deterministic) PDA.

Since every regular language can always be recognized by a DFA (which is trivially also a valid DPDA that simply never uses its stack), every regular language is guaranteed accepted by some DPDA.

"Any context-free language," "any NPDA-accepted language" (these are the same, broader class, and DPDA is a strictly weaker/smaller class), and "any decidable language" (a vastly larger class, including languages that aren't even context-free) are all too broad to be guaranteed DPDA-acceptable.

Answer: Any regular language.

text: Consider a finite state machine (FSM) with one input [latex] X [/latex] and one output [latex] f [/latex], represented by the given state transition table. The minimum number of states required to realize this FSM is _________. (Answer in integer)
solution:
Group states by their immediate output behavior first: states with outputs [latex](f_0,f_1)=(0,0)[/latex] are [latex]\{A,B,C,E\}[/latex]; [latex](1,0)[/latex] are [latex]\{D,H\}[/latex]; [latex](1,1)[/latex] is [latex]\{F\}[/latex]; [latex](0,1)[/latex] is [latex]\{G\}[/latex] — four initial groups.

Refine [latex]\{A,B,C,E\}[/latex] by checking which group each state's next-states fall into: [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]C[/latex] both go to (group-of-[latex]F[/latex], group-of-[latex]\{A,B,C,E\}[/latex]) on [latex](X{=}0,X{=}1)[/latex], while [latex]B[/latex] and [latex]E[/latex] both go to (group-of-[latex]\{D,H\}[/latex], group-of-[latex]\{A,B,C,E\}[/latex]). So this group splits into [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex] and [latex]\{B,E\}[/latex].

Checking again with the new, finer partition [latex]\{A,C\},\{B,E\},\{D,H\},\{F\},\{G\}[/latex]: every state's next-state signature now matches consistently within its own group (e.g. both [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]C[/latex] go to [latex]F[/latex] on [latex]0[/latex] and into [latex]\{B,E\}[/latex] on [latex]1[/latex]; both [latex]D[/latex] and [latex]H[/latex] go to [latex]G[/latex] on [latex]0[/latex] and into [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex] on [latex]1[/latex]) — so the partition is stable and no further splitting occurs.

Final equivalence classes: [latex]\{A,C\},\{B,E\},\{D,H\},\{F\},\{G\}[/latex] — [latex]5[/latex] classes.

Consider the following two languages over the alphabet [latex]\{a, b, c\}[/latex], where [latex]m[/latex] and [latex]n[/latex] are natural numbers:

[latex]L_2 = \{ a^m b^n c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1 \}[/latex]

solution:
[latex]L_1=\{a^mb^mc^{m+n}\mid m,n\ge1\}[/latex]: this requires two separate comparisons tied to the same value [latex]m[/latex] — matching [latex]a[/latex]'s against [latex]b[/latex]'s exactly (using up a stack), and independently comparing the [latex]c[/latex]-count against that same [latex]m[/latex] again. A single-stack PDA can only "remember and compare" one running count at a time; once the stack is used up matching [latex]a[/latex]'s against [latex]b[/latex]'s, the value of [latex]m[/latex] is no longer available to compare against the [latex]c[/latex]'s. This mirrors the classic non-context-free pattern [latex]a^nb^nc^n[/latex]. [latex]L_1[/latex] is not context-free.

[latex]L_2=\{a^mb^nc^{m+n}\mid m,n\ge1\}[/latex]: here the [latex]c[/latex]-count only needs to match the combined total of [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]b[/latex]'s (not two separate comparisons). A single stack handles this easily: push one symbol for every [latex]a[/latex] and every [latex]b[/latex] (treating them the same way), then pop one symbol per [latex]c[/latex], accepting if the stack empties exactly when the input ends. [latex]L_2[/latex] is context-free.

Answer: L1 is not context-free but L2 is context-free.

Consider the following two languages over the alphabet [latex]\{a, b\}[/latex]:

[latex]L_2 = \{ \alpha \beta \alpha \mid \alpha \in \{a\}^+ \text{ and } \beta \in \{a, b\}^+ \}[/latex]

solution:
[latex]L_1=\{\alpha\beta\alpha\mid\alpha,\beta\in\{a,b\}^+\}[/latex] (α completely unrestricted): checking membership genuinely requires comparing an arbitrary-length prefix against an arbitrary-length suffix for exact equality. For instance, "[latex]abbaab[/latex]" is in [latex]L_1[/latex] (via [latex]\alpha=ab,\beta=ba[/latex]) even though its very first and very last characters differ — so no bounded "look at a few characters" trick works; a finite automaton cannot carry the unbounded memory needed to remember an arbitrarily long prefix for later comparison. [latex]L_2[/latex] is regular.

Answer: L1 is not regular but L2 is regular.

text: A regular language [latex]L[/latex] is accepted by a non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) with [latex]n[/latex] states. Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE?
solution:
For a regular language [latex]L[/latex] accepted by some [latex]n[/latex]-state NFA, recall two standard facts: (1) subset construction always produces an equivalent DFA with at most [latex]2^n[/latex] states, and (2) NFA/DFA state counts for a given language are not unique — smaller equivalent automata can certainly exist.

- "[latex]L[/latex] may have an accepting NFA with [latex]< n[/latex] states": could well be true (this [latex]n[/latex]-state NFA might not be minimal), so calling it FALSE is incorrect — it's a true possibility, not a false statement.
- "[latex]L[/latex] may have an accepting DFA with [latex]< n[/latex] states": also entirely possible depending on the language, so this is also true (not false).
- "There exists a DFA with [latex]\le 2^n[/latex] states accepting [latex]L[/latex]": guaranteed true by subset construction — so this is also true, not false.
- "Every DFA that accepts L has [latex]> 2^n[/latex] states": this directly contradicts the subset-construction guarantee (a DFA with at most [latex]2^n[/latex] states always exists) — so this statement is definitely FALSE.

Answer: "Every DFA that accepts L has more than [latex]2^n[/latex] states" is the FALSE statement.
